# Microbes and their hosts

> *Most people carry potential pathogens without harm. Why does the same organism make one person ill
> and leave another well, and when illness does follow, how much of the damage comes from the microbe
> and how much from the host's own response?*

## Four terms that are often confused {#sec-host-words}

General pathology gave you the vocabulary of tissue injury. Microbiology adds four terms that students
often use interchangeably, although they describe different states.

| Term | What it means | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Contamination** | Microbes are present on a surface but not multiplying | Bacteria on an unwashed hand |
| **Colonisation** | Microbes live and multiply at a site without causing damage | *Staphylococcus aureus* in the nose of a healthy person |
| **Infection** | Microbes multiply in tissue, and the host responds | Bacteria multiplying in a wound, with local inflammation |
| **Disease** | The host is damaged enough to produce signs and symptoms | Fever, pain and swelling from that wound |

Infection does not always lead to disease. In one Singapore study, 42 of 245 healthy children
attending childcare centres (17.1%) had enterovirus in their saliva with no symptoms of hand, foot and
mouth disease at the time of sampling [@min2021hfmd]. A person who harbours and can transmit an
organism without being ill is a **carrier**.

## The microbiota {#sec-host-microbiota}

The **microbiota** is the community of microbes that normally lives on and in the body: in the colon,
the mouth, the skin, the upper airway and the vagina. Its composition differs between sites because
each site offers different conditions. Stomach acid, the dryness and salt of skin, and the near-absence
of oxygen in the colon each select for different organisms.

Resident microbes contribute to defence and to nutrition in several ways:

- They occupy attachment sites and consume nutrients that incoming organisms would need, a protection
  called **colonisation resistance**.
- Some produce substances that inhibit competitors.
- Their presence helps the immune system develop and stay regulated.
- Gut bacteria ferment dietary fibre the host cannot digest, and synthesise vitamin K and several B
  vitamins.

Disturbing the community removes this protection. A course of antibacterial treatment, for example,
can allow *Clostridioides difficile*, which tolerates the disturbance, to multiply in the colon and
cause diarrhoea. Vaginal candidiasis after antibacterial treatment follows the same logic.

::: {.callout-important}
## A common idea, corrected: "microbes are germs, and germs are harmful"
Children as young as seven describe microorganisms as essentially harmful [@byrne2011children], and
the idea persists into adult life. Pathogens are in fact a small minority, and the organisms behind
most human infections are often the same ones that live on us harmlessly most of the time. Usually the
organism is unchanged; what changes is the site it reaches, or the state of the host.
:::

## When a resident becomes a problem {#sec-host-opportunism}

An **opportunistic pathogen** is an organism of low virulence that causes disease when the host's
defences are impaired, or when it reaches a site it does not normally occupy. Three situations recur:

1. A barrier is breached: skin is cut, a catheter crosses it, or surgery opens the bowel so that gut
   organisms reach the peritoneal cavity.
2. Defences are weakened: **neutropenia** (a low neutrophil count) after chemotherapy, impaired
   cell-mediated immunity in advanced HIV infection, or impaired neutrophil function in diabetes.
3. The microbiota is disturbed, as described above.

A **strict pathogen**, by contrast, causes disease in people with normal defences: *Mycobacterium
tuberculosis*, *Salmonella* Typhi and influenza virus do not need a weakened host. Because the boundary
is not sharp, a more useful question than "is this organism a pathogen?" is "what does it take, in
this host, for this organism to cause damage?"

## Where the damage comes from {#sec-host-drf}

The **damage-response framework** of Casadevall and Pirofski answers that question
[@casadevall2003damage]. It holds that disease is defined by host damage, and that damage can come
from the microbe, from the host's response, or from both. If damage is plotted against the strength of
the host response, different organisms give differently shaped curves.

<div data-island="damage-response" data-src="/diagrams/damage-response.yml"></div>

Students usually find the right-hand side of these curves surprising, because it shows that a vigorous
immune response is not always beneficial. Three examples recur in this book. In **toxic shock
syndrome**, a **superantigen**, a toxin that activates a large fraction of T cells at once, triggers
cytokine release that causes **hypotension** (dangerously low blood pressure). In **rheumatic fever**, antibodies
raised against *Streptococcus pyogenes* cross-react with heart tissue weeks after the infection has
cleared. In tuberculosis, much of the destruction of lung tissue is the work of the immune response
to bacteria it cannot eliminate. [*Gram-positive cocci*](../microbes/gram-positive-cocci.qmd) returns to
the first two.

General pathology makes the same point about inflammation: a response that protects in proportion can
harm in excess. The immunology block supplies the mechanisms.

## Host factors {#sec-host-factors}

When two people meet the same organism and only one becomes ill, the reasons usually lie with the
host. Casadevall and Pirofski group them under the mnemonic **MISTEACHING**: Microbiota, Inoculum,
Sex, Temperature, Environment, Age, Chance, History of exposure, Immunity, Nutrition and Genetics
[@casadevall2018misteaching].

Three of these matter most at this stage. The **inoculum**, the number of organisms received, affects
both whether disease follows and how quickly it begins; for some organisms a few cells are enough,
while for others many thousands must be swallowed. Immunity includes both the specific immunity left
by earlier exposure or vaccination and the general competence of the defences: neutropenia, impaired
cell-mediated immunity and **asplenia** (absence of a functioning spleen) each leave characteristic
gaps. Other conditions shift the balance as well. Diabetes is the clearest local example: among
patients with melioidosis in Singapore between 2003 and 2014, 56.7% had diabetes, against 19.3% of the
general population of similar age [@pang2018melioidosis].

## What a microbe has to do {#sec-host-steps}

To cause an infection, a microbe has to complete a sequence of steps. Anything it uses to complete
them is a **virulence factor**: a product or structure that helps it infect or damage a host. The
steps are:

1. Reach a surface and attach to it.
2. Invade beyond the surface, or stay on it and act from there.
3. Evade host defences long enough to multiply.
4. Obtain nutrients, iron in particular, which the host keeps bound to proteins.
5. Damage the host, directly or through the response it provokes.

Attachment explains **tropism**, the range of tissues or cells an organism can occupy. A microbe can
only settle where it finds the molecule it binds. This is why influenza virus infects cells lining the
airway and not skin, and why strains of *E. coli* that bind receptors in the urinary tract cause
urinary infection.

<div data-island="sorter" data-src="/diagrams/pathogenesis-sorter.yml"></div>

## Two meanings of "toxin" {#sec-host-toxins}

Students meet two things called toxins and often merge them, although they differ in almost every
respect.

<div data-island="contrast-pair" data-src="/diagrams/pair-exotoxin-endotoxin.yml"></div>

The difference has clinical consequences. Protein exotoxins can be inactivated and used as **toxoid**
vaccines, which is how tetanus and diphtheria are prevented. Lipopolysaccharide cannot, and the
inflammatory response it drives is central to the deterioration seen in severe Gram-negative
infection.

## The time course of infection {#sec-host-courses}

Infections differ in how they unfold over time, and the pattern often follows from the organism's
strategy.

| Pattern | What happens | Typical strategy |
|---|---|---|
| **Acute** | Rapid onset; the organism is cleared or the host dies | Multiply fast, transmit, move on |
| **Latent** | The organism persists silently and can reactivate | Survive inside cells, or in a site the immune response reaches poorly |
| **Chronic** | Infection and inflammation continue for months or years | Resist clearance; damage accumulates from the ongoing response |

Latency explains a clinical pattern you will meet repeatedly. An organism that persists where immune
surveillance is limited, or inside the cells meant to destroy it, can return when immunity falls,
sometimes decades later.

## Using this chapter in Part II {#sec-host-close}

For each organism in Part II, ask two questions. How does it damage the host: by destroying cells, by
toxins, by provoking a damaging inflammatory response, or by a combination? And where does it sit on
the damage-response curve? If most of the damage comes from the host's response, a weakened host may
show less visible disease, and removing the organism alone may not stop the damage.
